title: Degenerate Turing bifurcation and the birth of localised patterns in activator-inhibitor systems
abstract: Precise conditions are provided for the existence and criticality of Turing bifurcations in a general class of activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion equations on a one-dimensional infinite domain. The class includes generalised Schnakenberg and Brusselator models, as well as other models with cubic autocatalytic nonlinear terms. Previous numerical work suggests the existence of a bifurcation structure containing localised patterns due to the so-called homoclinic snaking mechanism. This paper provides explicit calculations to justify those results. Two distinct scalings of parameters that lead to tractable normal-form coefficients are considered in the limit that the diffusion ratio $δ\to 0$. First, under a small-parameter scaling, the Turing bifurcation is shown to be always subcritical. Second, a large-parameter scaling reveals the Turing bifurcation to be supercritical, leading, by continuity, to the existence of a codimension-two degenerate bifurcation. The sign of a 5th-order normal form coefficient is also computed, which is shown to have the correct sign for the local birth of homoclinic snaking. For the case of the Brusselator, two such codimension-two points can be found explicitly, as can the leading-order expression for the Maxwell point, in a parameter wedge about which localised patterns emerge. Numerical results are found to be consistent with the theory.
summary: This theoretical paper rigorously analyzes the conditions for pattern formation in activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion systems undergoing a Turing bifurcation. By developing high-order normal form theory, the authors determine that the bifurcation can be degenerate, leading to the formation of localized structures via a homoclinic snaking mechanism. This work provides deep mathematical insight into pattern selection in non-equilibrium physical models.
main_problem: The paper provides precise mathematical conditions for the existence and criticality of Turing bifurcations in general activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion systems, focusing on the degenerate bifurcation leading to localized patterns.
main_result: The analysis shows that depending on the parameter scaling ($\delta 	o 0$), the bifurcation can be subcritical or supercritical, leading to a codimension-two degenerate bifurcation characterized by the sign of a fifth-order normal form coefficient.
method: The authors employ weakly nonlinear perturbation theory, deriving and analyzing the normal form equations up to the fifth order to determine the stability and nature of the pattern formation transition.
model_or_system: The study concerns two-component activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion equations, exemplified by generalized Schnakenberg and Brusselator models, defined on a one-dimensional infinite domain.
key_observables: Turing bifurcation, localized patterns (homoclinic snaking), subcritical/supercritical nature of the bifurcation, and the Maxwell point.
important_parameters: The diffusion ratio $\delta$, and the parameters governing the reaction kinetics ($\alpha,  eta, \gamma$, etc.).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on Taylor expansion and the assumption that the system can be reduced to an amplitude equation via multiple scales, particularly in the limit $\delta 	o 0$.
figures_summary: Figure 1(a) illustrates the dispersion relation at a Turing bifurcation, while Figure 1(b) shows the energy functional $E(A)$ used to define the Maxwell point condition.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general conditions for Turing instability (T1 & T2), then derives the amplitude equation, and finally performs high-order normal form calculations to determine the coefficients governing the degenerate bifurcation and the emergence of localized structures.
why_interesting: While focused on classical reaction-diffusion systems, the mathematical techniques used—analyzing pattern formation via bifurcation theory and normal forms—are foundational to understanding phase transitions and pattern selection in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
